name: Process List, Handles & Loaded DLLs (Memory Forensics)
os_min: N/A (RAM capture, any Windows version supported by the analysis tool)
location: Not a disk location - reconstructed from a RAM acquisition (raw memory image, hibernation file, or crash dump) using Volatility 3's windows.pslist, windows.pstree, windows.psscan, windows.dlllist, and windows.handles plugins.
purpose: Reconstructs which processes were running at the moment of memory capture, their parent-child relationships, loaded modules, and open handles, by parsing EPROCESS/ETHREAD kernel structures and the process PEB directly out of the memory image. Because several of these plugins locate processes by different mechanisms, comparing their output is the primary way to catch a process a rootkit tried to hide.
key_fields: windows.pslist - walks the kernel's doubly-linked PsActiveProcessHead list (via each EPROCESS's ActiveProcessLinks) to enumerate PID, PPID, process name, thread count, handle count, and create/exit time
windows.pstree - same enumeration as pslist, rendered as a parent-child tree using the recorded PPID/creation-time relationships

windows.psscan - does not trust the active-process list; scans the entire memory image for pool allocations matching the EPROCESS pool tag/structure signature, so it also surfaces unlinked and recently terminated processes
windows.dlllist - per process, walks the PEB's InLoadOrderModuleList (a list of _LDR_DATA_TABLE_ENTRY structures) to list loaded module path, base address, and size

windows.handles - per process, enumerates the open handle table and reports handle type (Process, Thread, Key, Event, Mutant, Token, File, Section, etc.), the target object, and access rights; filterable by object type
PID / PPID - process and parent process ID (both are simply reused numbers in Windows and can be spoofed by an attacker's chosen parent)
Offset (virtual) - the EPROCESS structure's memory address, useful for direct correlation between plugin outputs and for volshell follow-up
normal_baseline: pslist, pstree, and psscan agree on the same set of processes and PIDs; every process has a plausible parent (e.g. explorer.exe under a userinit/logon chain, svchost.exe under services.exe), loaded DLLs match what the executable and its known dependencies would load, and handle counts are unremarkable for the process type.
anomalies: A process visible in windows.psscan's raw pool scan but absent from windows.pslist's linked-list walk - the classic signature of a rootkit that used Direct Kernel Object Manipulation (DKOM) to unlink the EPROCESS from PsActiveProcessHead while the process's threads kept running

A process name mimicking a legitimate system binary but running from an unexpected path (e.g. svchost.exe outside %SystemRoot%\System32) or with an implausible parent (e.g. lsass.exe or services.exe not spawned by wininit.exe)
windows.dlllist showing a module loaded from a suspicious or non-standard path (temp directory, user profile) inside an otherwise legitimate process, consistent with DLL injection

A process with very few or zero entries in windows.dlllist despite being a normal Windows executable that should have a substantial import list - can indicate manual PEB/module-list unlinking to hide an injected or reflectively-loaded module

windows.handles showing a process holding a handle to lsass.exe with access rights consistent with memory-reading (credential dumping), or holding handles to another unrelated process with PROCESS_VM_WRITE/PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD rights (injection primitives)

PPID mismatch such as a PID reused by an unrelated later process (PPID spoofing), or a shell/office-application process tree where a document viewer or browser is the direct parent of cmd.exe or powershell.exe

psscan surfacing a process that has already exited (terminated) but whose EPROCESS pool allocation has not yet been reused - itself not anomalous, but the executable path, command line, and DLL list of that terminated process can still be extracted and are worth checking against other indicators
parsing_tools: Volatility 3 (Volatility Foundation) - windows.pslist, windows.pstree, windows.psscan, windows.dlllist, windows.handles
volshell (Volatility 3 interactive shell) for manual EPROCESS/PEB inspection
anti_forensic_notes: Volatility 3 does not ship a direct equivalent of Volatility 2's psxview cross-view plugin; the cross-view check that psxview automated must be performed manually by diffing the PID sets returned by windows.pslist (linked-list walk) against windows.psscan (raw pool scan) - a PID present in the latter but missing from the former is the strongest single indicator of DKOM-based process hiding. Because psscan finds EPROCESS structures by pool signature rather than by following any list, an attacker who fully unlinks a process from every kernel list Volatility can walk still cannot prevent that process's memory pool footprint from being found by psscan, short of also zeroing/overwriting the EPROCESS pool tag itself, which would typically crash the running process's scheduling.
